en: Preface to the Easy-to-Understand Verse-by-Verse Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of Prajñāpāramitā The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* is the heart of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*,
the essential outline of its six hundred fascicles, the marrow and bones of the five thousand volumes of the Great Canon,
and the fundamental source for becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch. Thus, those who wish to comprehend birth and death [must study it].
For those who seek liberation from saṃsāra, there is no other path than this. This is why its recitation and upholding are so flourishing, filling the seas that surround this world.
Yet, though those who recite it are many, those who truly understand it are few. It is not because this sutra is difficult to comprehend, nor is it because sentient beings are particularly ignorant;
the trouble lies in the lack of a good commentary, which causes confusion of the ears and eyes. Indeed, this...
Since the sutras first entered the Middle Kingdom, there have been no fewer than several dozen schools of commentators.
Yet some take indirect paths through the lost scriptures to express their own personal views;
their distance from the Buddha’s original intent is more than a thousand li. Even those whose interpretations accord with the meaning of the sutras, moreover—

Alternatively, some provide only a brief summary of the general meaning with sparse explanations of the words and phrases; this makes it difficult for beginners to comprehend and is highly inconvenient.
There are those who, perceiving this flaw, have sought to rectify it. Yet others boast of their vast knowledge and vie for ornate expression, citing distant precedents and extensive authorities;

thus, while their verbose language becomes increasingly complex, the true essence becomes ever more obscure. Those who read such works are left bewildered, not knowing what is being said. This [work] clarifies this very sūtra.

Those who have followed this path are few indeed. (Sheng) Compassionate toward this suffering, he thus gave rise to a great vow, swearing to compose an excellent commentary to enlighten the ignorant masses.

Thereupon, he extensively searched through various commentaries, closing his door in pure contemplation. He applied himself to discernment with utmost precision and was exceedingly cautious in what to adopt and what to reject.
He followed that which was good and corrected that which was not. After three years of diligent study and reflection, he was finally able to complete the work.

The previous commentaries were overly fragmented in their structural analysis; therefore, I have generally adopted a more concise approach. This work is neither redundant nor omissive, though it is both simple and plain.

I have taken only what clarifies the principle, having no concern for whether the phrasing is crude, as my aim is for everyone to understand easily. Once the book was completed, I titled it *Jùjiě Yìzhī* (Phrase-by-Phrase Explanation for Easy Understanding).
I retained the original title of my previous commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and did not change it, because...
This has indeed been my long-standing aspiration. Now, since Bodhidharma came from the West, he did not rely on written words;
he pointed directly at the human mind, so that by seeing one’s nature, one becomes a Buddha. Thus, these scriptures are like dregs, and commentaries are even more superfluous appendages.
Yet, I have not shunned exhaustion nor declined the reproach of others in composing these "snake-foot" words, for I truly desire that those of beginner’s capacity may—
Awakening is simply knowing. It is like obtaining a precious raft when lost at a ford; thus, the sea of suffering is easily crossed and the further shore is easily ascended.
Those who escape the cycle of rebirth and comprehend birth and death likely do so more often than not because of this.
My earnest heart truly finds it difficult to restrain itself. Someone may say: "You have elucidated this great principle most excellently, surpassing others."
The intervening difference in wealth, honor, fame, and achievement is ten thousand times a hundred millionfold. Yet how would I dare speak thus?
It is merely intended as a small aid for those newly learning, following the principle that "to travel far one begins from near; to climb high one starts from the low."

Preface by the Layman Wang Zesheng on the "Easy-to-Understand Sentence-by-Sentence Explanation of the Heart Sutra of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā," composed on an auspicious day in the third month of the Jiashen year, the twenty-ninth year of the Qianlong era.
*Mahā* is a Sanskrit term; in Chinese it is translated as "Great. *Prajñā* is also a Sanskrit term; in Chinese it is translated as "Wisdom.
*Pāramitā* is likewise a Sanskrit term; in Chinese it is translated as "Reaching the Other Shore.

This is because the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) for sentient beings is likened to a vast ocean, while the bliss of the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa* is established as the "other shore"; thus, wisdom must be employed as the boat.
Only by means of this raft can one cross over the sea of suffering and reach the other shore.

"Mind" (citta) refers to the core of the Great Prajñāpāramitā, encompassing the profound meanings of its six hundred fascicles; it is like a person’s single mind, which can govern the four limbs and all the bones and joints.
"Sūtra" (sūtra) means a path; it is the path for entering the Way. This scripture is thus spoken of as being vast and...
Wisdom. It is the path by which the Buddhas reach the other shore, and this single fascicle is the very heart of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras;
it is indeed the essential summary of the six hundred fascicles. △ This sūtra is titled according to its singular dharma.
Taking the characteristic of emptiness as its essence, contemplative observation as its primary principle, the deliverance from suffering as its function, and the Mahāyāna as its doctrinal aspect.

The commentary on the verse says:
This spark of spirit ascends the Way; it is only because of chasing after delusions that one falls into the dust.
If you now wish to see the path back home, awaken to the Heart Sutra and the Eye of the Way will open.

△ [Section on Manifestation] This section on manifesting the sutra is divided into two major parts: Exoteric and Esoteric. From the beginning up to *sambodhi* (Perfect Enlightenment) constitutes the first part.

The "Manifest Teaching" (Khyen-sö) is divided into seven sections. From the section on "Knowing by Oneself" (Zi-gu-zhi) to the end constitutes the "Secret Teaching" (Mi-sö), which is further divided into three sections.
Together, these comprise ten divisions. First:

The Section on the Bodhisattva’s Cultivation and Realization (*Bodhisattva-sādhanādhigama-bhāga*). (These ten divisions were categorized by the Master Kuan; we follow his arrangement here. The other minor subdivisions are numerous and cumbersome, and have thus been deleted en masse.)
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
"Bodhisattva" is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the language of China, it means "one who awakens sentient beings. Avalokiteśvara is the same as Guanyin (Observing the World's Sounds).
This is because, by employing supreme wisdom, he observes that his own mind is pure, perfectly penetrating and unimpeded, and thus dwells with ease and mastery.
Therefore, he is also named Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
When practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā, "practitioner" (xingzhe) refers to one who engages in cultivation.
"Profound Prajñā" refers to the Prajñā of the true mark (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-prajñā*); it is not the coarse mind or shallow wisdom.

This is what is observed; therefore, it is called "profound. *Prajñā* means wisdom, which is that mind of original enlightenment and original luminosity possessed equally by all sentient beings and Buddhas.
*Pāramitā* means "reaching the other shore. When this Bodhisattva practices profound and vast wisdom and attains the other shore of *nirvāṇa*, [this is the perfection of wisdom].
"To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty": "perceive" (*zhào*) means to contemplate.
"To perceive" (*zhàojiàn*) means to see through them. "Aggregates" (*yùn*) means accumulations. "Five" refers to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Form" (*sè*) refers to the physical body. "Sensation" (*shòu*) refers to reception. "Perception" (*xiǎng*) refers to conceptualization. "Mental formations" (*xíng*) refer to volitional activity.
The *vijñāna* (consciousness) discriminates. There are these five components which accumulate and cover over [reality], such that one cannot see through them.
One falsely identifies the physical body as the self; for this reason, one wanders in saṃsāra through long kalpas with no prospect of escape.

Only when a Bodhisattva’s cultivation of *prajñā* (wisdom) has become profound can they spontaneously engage in contemplative observation, seeing clearly within their own body that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these...
The five aggregates are originally non-existent; they all belong to the realm of delusion and are not real.

Know that there is not a single dharma that does not arise through the illusory nature, yet there is not a single dharma that is not fundamentally empty by nature. Question: How can the five aggregates all be empty? Answer:
It is like the head, eyes, brain, and marrow—all may be given away as offerings. Even if one were to cut, slice, or invade [the body], [it would be no different].
Ling: To be entirely without anger or resentment is the emptiness of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
When encountering all objects and phenomena, if the mind does not grasp them—seeing as if not seeing—it is the emptiness of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

If one does not reflect on the past, does not anticipate the future, and has no mind in the present, it is the emptiness of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). If one is not turned by external things and does not follow them...
When the environment shifts, there is no movement at all; this is the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
When one sees all objects and phenomena without any discrimination, viewing them with equanimity, this is the emptiness of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Once the emptiness of the aggregates is realized, one is able to uproot the foundation of saṃsāra and sever the seeds of birth and death, thereby attaining eternal liberation from the suffering realms of this Sahā world.
"Deliverance from all suffering and calamity.

"Deliverance" means liberation. "All" refers to the general totality. "All suffering and calamity" refers to every kind of affliction, hardship, and disaster experienced by sentient beings in the world.
Since the Bodhisattva has realized the emptiness of the five aggregates as being themselves, they have already transcended them.
This is the ocean of suffering of birth and death. Furthermore, out of compassion for sentient beings lost in delusion— who are shrouded by the five aggregates and unable to pierce through them,
thereby undergoing manifold sufferings— he has preached this Dharma-gate of Prajñā, so that all sentient beings may hear and practice it,
thereby delivering themselves from their hardships and calamities, like boarding a great ship to cross over.
Sentient beings are sent across the ocean of suffering, only after they have ascended directly to the other shore.
The phrase "Avalokiteśvara" serves as the general heading for the entire text. The phrase "practicing deeply" explains the cause, which is the internal contemplation one cultivates;
the phrase "perceiving clearly" explains the fruit, which is the attainment of sovereign mastery; and the phrase "delivering all" explains the Bodhisattva who has realized this realization.
These three phrases serve as a general summary for the entire text.

"The preceding section describes the meritorious practices of Avalokiteśvara in saving sentient beings at the time Ānanda compiled the Piṭaka of the Sūtras; this constitutes the 'Separate Introduction' (Bie xu). The following section..."

Beginning from Śāriputra, this is the section where Avalokiteśvara answers the questions posed by Śāriputra. Part Two: The Section on the Correct Meaning of the Emptiness of Form. Śāriputra: [The text continues: "Śāriputra," etc. (The following is the beginning of the dialogue: "Śāriputra, form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Form is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than form. And so forth. Śāriputra: "O Noble One, how should one regard the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*? Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "Śāriputra, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they perceive that all five aggregates are empty, and they deliver sentient beings from all suffering and distress. Śāriputra: "How should one regard form? Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Form is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than form. What is true of form is likewise true of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra: "How should one regard emptiness? Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "Emptiness is characterized by neither arising nor ceasing, neither defilement nor purity, neither increase nor decrease. Within emptiness, there is no form, no sensation, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness. No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena; no sight-organ element up to and including no mind-consciousness element; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no aging-and-death and no extinction of aging-and-death. There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment, and even no non-attainment. Therefore, Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies upon *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear. Having transcended all inverted dreams, they realize ultimate *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying upon *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Śāriputra: "Excellent, excellent, O Noble One! What you have said is truly so. Because the *prajñāpāramitā* spoken by the Noble One is the great mantra, the mantra of great knowledge, the unsurpassed mantra, the peerless mantra, it can extinguish all suffering. It is true and not false. Therefore, one should know the *prajñāpāramitā* mantra as it is spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "Śāriputra, if a good man or good woman wishes to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should thus observe all phenomena with correct wisdom and ultimately attain *nirvāṇa*. Śāriputra: "Well said, O Noble One! Thus ends the second chapter, the Section on the Correct Meaning of the Emptiness of Form. Part Three: The Section on the True Nature of the Five Aggregates. 'Mental formations' are the nature of volitional activity; therefore, they are called 'mental formations. 'Consciousness' is the nature of cognition; therefore, it is called 'consciousness. Śāriputra: "O Noble One, what is the meaning of 'emptiness'? Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "Śāriputra, 'emptiness' means being devoid of self and what belongs to a self; therefore, it is called 'emptiness. Śāriputra: "O Noble One, what is the meaning of 'neither arising nor ceasing'? Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "Śāriputra, because all phenomena are originally unborn, they do not arise; because they do not arise, they do not cease. Therefore, they are called 'neither arising nor ceasing. Śāriputra: "O Noble One, what is the meaning of 'neither defilement nor purity'? Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:

"Śāriputra, because all phenomena are originally pure, they are neither defiled nor pure. Therefore, they are called 'neither defilement nor purity. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "Śāriputra, because all phenomena are originally equal, they neither increase nor decrease. Therefore, they are called 'neither increase nor decrease. *Śāri* is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the Chinese language, it is translated as "crane" (*shūlù*). This bird has keen eyesight, and the Venerable One’s mother had eyes like those of this bird;
therefore, he was named Śāriputra (Son of Śāri). He is also called Śāripuṭra (Crane Son). Among the disciples of the Buddha, he was foremost in wisdom.
In the version translated by the Venerable Dharmarakṣa, it says: "At that time, the World-Honored One was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, having entered into the profound light..."
The Illumination of Samādhi. Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"If there are those who wish to practice and study this profound gateway of Prajñāpāramitā, how should they practice and study it?
The Bodhisattva, sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, proclaimed the essential meaning within the Prajñā section, saying: "Śāriputra, listen well. [O] Stainless..."
The Master’s commentary states: "‘House’ refers to a dwelling; ‘the original essence within the house’ refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is a great error. Form is not different from emptiness.

Those who wish to cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should clarify the correct meaning of the identity of form and emptiness. For example, it is said that the body composed of the four great elements is like an illusion."
Regarding form (*rūpa*): the true essence of *prajñā* is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Ordinary beings cling to the characteristics of form and thus perceive it as being different from emptiness.
They do not realize that form arises from delusion and returns to extinction through delusion; thus, its very characteristic of arising is entirely the characteristic of extinction.
Since it is the characteristic of extinction, how is it different from the characteristic of emptiness? Form and emptiness are fundamentally no different in essence. This is because...
Form is like ice and emptiness is like water. Just as one realizes that ice exists because of water, one knows that form is not different from emptiness.
Why is this? Form arises from emptiness; thus, form certainly cannot be grasped.
Emptiness is not different from form.
The heterodox hold a view of annihilation, claiming there is neither cause nor effect; the followers of the Two Vehicles cling to a partial emptiness, extinguishing the body and dissolving wisdom.
Thus they perceive emptiness as being distinct from form, failing to realize that the ultimate void embraces the ultimate reality of the world, and that the ultimate non-existence...
Yet, within this, the ultimate existence of the world—emptiness and form—are essentially no different. For emptiness is like water, and form is like ice.
Just as one realizes that water is produced by the melting of ice, one knows that emptiness is not distinct from form. Why is this so?
Emptiness is manifested through form; how, then, could emptiness itself be grasped?
Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form.
Although it is said that they are not different, this still implies two distinct entities in opposition. In reality, form is not form characterized by obstruction.
The entirety of illusory form is emptiness; there is no emptiness apart from form. Emptiness is not an emptiness of annihilation;
the great function of true emptiness is precisely form; there is no form apart from emptiness. It is like ice being water and water being ice.
One need not maintain the dualistic views of form and emptiness; for there is not only no form, but also no emptiness. This...
It is empty of intrinsic nature.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
It is not only the aggregate of form that is thus empty; even the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Furthermore, one should contemplate emptiness in this way: it is non-different from [the aggregates] and is itself emptiness.
Only after this can the five aggregates be seen as entirely empty. This is because the aggregates lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for they are fundamentally illusory existents;
therefore, they are all empty. Emptiness has no separate essence, for there is nothing that is not its essence; therefore, they are all truly real.

This section shows people that the five aggregates are empty, providing a detailed exposition of the phrase "practice the profound" in accordance with the meaning of the word "should observe. III. The Section on the Arising and Ceasing of the Three Emptinesses. Śāriputra, [the Buddha said: The meaning of the word "should observe" (應觀) is as follows: it means one should contemplate that the three types of emptiness—namely, the emptiness of the internal, the emptiness of the external, and the emptiness of the internal and external—are themselves empty. This is because all phenomena arise from conditions and are devoid of intrinsic nature. Therefore, one should contemplate that these three types of emptiness are ultimately empty. This is the meaning of the word "should observe. As for the phrase "practice the profound" (行深): "profound" (深) refers to the ultimate reality (勝義諦). To practice this reality is called "practicing the profound. Furthermore, "profound" refers to the fact that all phenomena are beyond conceptualization and verbal expression; to enter into such a state is called "practicing the profound. Moreover, "profound" refers to the fact that all phenomena are originally quiescent and non-arising; to realize this is called "practicing the profound. Thus, by practicing the profound, one realizes the emptiness of the three types of emptiness. This is the meaning of the phrase "practice the profound. Regarding the title "The Section on the Arising and Ceasing of the Three Emptinesses": "three emptinesses" refers to the emptiness of the internal, the emptiness of the external, and the emptiness of the internal and external. "Arising and ceasing" means that these three types of emptiness are subject to production and extinction. However, because they are themselves empty, there is no true arising or ceasing. Therefore, it is called "the arising and ceasing of the three emptinesses. This section explains that although the three types of emptiness appear to arise and cease according to conditions, their essential nature is ultimately empty and quiescent. This is why it is titled "The Section on the Arising and Ceasing of the Three Emptinesses. Śāriputra, the Buddha addressed him as follows: "Śāriputra, form is empty; emptiness is form. Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. What is form is emptiness; what is emptiness is form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. In this passage, the Buddha first states that form is empty. Why? Because form lacks intrinsic nature. Since it lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty. However, this emptiness does not mean that form is annihilated; rather, it means that form is devoid of self-nature. Therefore, it is said that "emptiness is form. Next, he says that form is not different from emptiness. Why? Because apart from form, there is no separate emptiness. Therefore, it is said that "form is not different from emptiness. Furthermore, he says that emptiness is not different from form. Why? Because apart from emptiness, there is no separate form. Therefore, it is said that "emptiness is not different from form. Finally, he says that what is form is emptiness, and what is emptiness is form. This means that form and emptiness are identical and non-dual. One cannot say that form exists while emptiness does not, nor can one say that emptiness exists while form does not. They are mutually inclusive and inseparable. This is the meaning of the teaching that form is empty and emptiness is form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. This means that the remaining four aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are likewise empty. Just as form is empty, so too are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness empty. Therefore, it is said that "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. By thus explaining that the five aggregates are empty, the Buddha reveals that all phenomena are devoid of self and belong to the category of the empty. This is the meaning of the teaching that the five aggregates are empty. Therefore, one should contemplate that the five aggregates are empty and practice the profound. By doing so, one will be able to transcend birth and death and attain liberation. This is the essential meaning of this section. It is titled "The Section on the Arising and Ceasing of the Three Emptinesses" because it specifically explains the arising and ceasing of the three types of emptiness. Through this, one understands that although phenomena appear to arise and cease, their ultimate nature is empty and quiescent. This is the core intent of the teaching. Thus ends the third section: The Section on the Arising and Ceasing of the Three Emptinesses. Śāriputra. The Buddha addressed him as follows: "Śāriputra, form is empty; emptiness is form. Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. What is form is emptiness; what is emptiness is form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. This concludes the detailed exposition of the meaning of the word "should observe" and the practice of the profound. It serves to demonstrate that the five aggregates are empty. It is titled "The Section on the Arising and Ceasing of the Three Emptinesses" to show that although the three types of emptiness arise and cease according to conditions, their essential nature is ultimately empty and quiescent. Śāriputra, I tell you again:
these dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness.
Even the true reality (*tathatā*) of the five aggregates and all dharmas is such that there is not even "emptiness" to be named; how much less so [anything else]?
There are names and characteristics such as arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease;
yet there is neither arising nor ceasing.
True emptiness is fundamentally without origination. It is not a point of initial conjunction through conditions that appears illusorily as having arisen—this is the analogy for the truth.

Even emptiness has no cessation. It is not that which is separated from conditions or from the future limit. That which undergoes transformation and destruction and possesses extinction is a mere analogy.

It is like a jewel manifesting five colors; yet the substance of the jewel has never undergone birth. When the five colors suddenly vanish, the substance of the jewel has likewise never undergone extinction.
Neither defiled nor pure.
"Defiled" refers to the dust of afflictions; through the binding karma of defiled conditions, one undergoes the cycle of rebirth in the six realms, which constitutes defilement.
True emptiness (*śūnyatā*) does not undergo such defilement. "Pure" refers to purity; by following pure conditions, one severs ignorance and achieves the purity of *nirvāṇa*.
Virtue is purity; yet even true emptiness does not receive purity.
It neither increases nor decreases.

Although the three wisdoms are equally perfected and the myriad practices are fully complete, these are nonetheless inherent within the essence itself; even in the state of a sage, nothing can be added.
It increases by not even a hair’s breadth. Even if one is among the six classes of mundane beings or submerged within the four modes of birth, all possess Buddha-nature;

while in the state of an ordinary being, it has never diminished by even the slightest amount. This is not a mere conjecture, for in the original state of true emptiness, such distinctions simply do not exist.
This section deduces that emptiness is fundamentally devoid of the aggregates.
Section Four: The Division of Phenomena Free from Defilement and Purity.
Therefore, within emptiness, there is no form; no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Because of this emptiness that is devoid of arising and ceasing, it is said that within true emptiness there is fundamentally no form-body, no sensation, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness.
These five aggregates are all empty. The character "wu" (無) in the following passages has two meanings:
first, it signifies that something is fundamentally non-existent; second, it signifies that something is not present.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

However, it is not merely that the five aggregates are empty; within true emptiness, there is also no eye-faculty, no ear-faculty, no nose-faculty, no tongue-faculty, no body-faculty, and no mind-faculty—the six faculties are likewise all empty.
There are no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects;
yet it is not merely that the six sense organs are empty.

For instance, the eye has the object of form, the ear has the object of sound, the nose has the object of odor, the tongue has the object of taste, the body has the object of touch, and the mind has the object of mental phenomena—all of these are entirely absent within true emptiness.
These six sense objects are likewise entirely empty. Since both the faculties and their objects are empty, this is what is called the emptiness of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
There is no realm of the eye, and so on, up to no realm of mental consciousness.
However, it is not merely that the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are empty;

within true emptiness, there are no six sense faculties (*indriya*)—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and likewise no six objects (*viṣaya*)—form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena. Furthermore, seeing is the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Hearing is ear-consciousness; smelling is nose-consciousness; tasting is tongue-consciousness; tactile sensation is body-consciousness; and discrimination is mind-consciousness.

Within true emptiness, there is likewise no realm of eye-consciousness, no realm of ear-consciousness, no realm of nose-consciousness, no realm of tongue-consciousness, no realm of body-consciousness, and even no realm of mind-consciousness. This is the absence of the six realms of consciousness.
Combining these constitutes the eighteen *dhātus* as emptiness. The above refers to the phenomena that lack a sentient being (*anātman*).

As for the "eighteen *dhātus*," they are the objective spheres of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses. Regarding the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*), this indicates the beginning and the end while omitting the middle;
it is an abbreviation used by the translator. Fearing that beginners might find it difficult to understand, I have here supplemented each point in detail.
It emerges.
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; and so on, up to no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.
Yet it is not only that the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are empty; even the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are likewise all empty. 10.
What are the two conditions? The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging."
Taking up [existence] conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; birth conditions old age and death. "Conditioning" refers to mutual dependence. As for "ignorance" (*avidyā*):
it means that the nature of wisdom is fundamentally luminous, wondrously profound, and exquisitely clear. Due to the sudden arising of delusive objects, it suddenly becomes obscured and darkened;
this is called ignorance. All afflictions of the past are of this nature; its essence is precisely delusion (*moha*), which causes one to lose...
This is the fundamental luminosity. To "enter into delusion" means that a practitioner, in past lives, performed various karmic actions;

these are called "formative activities" (*saṃskāra*). Because karma is created through delusion, there is ignorance (*avidyā*); because formative activities arise with ignorance as their cause, it is said that "ignorance conditions formative activities.

These two belong to the causes of the past life. Regarding "formative activities condition consciousness": when the obscured and darkened state wavers and fluctuates, one loses [the fundamental luminosity].

That [consciousness] is lucid and discerning; through its clinging to stillness, it gives rise to cognition. Thus, the transformation of wisdom (*jñāna*) is termed consciousness (*vijñāna*), which possesses the meaning of "discernment.

By means of the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome actions (*saṃskāra*), it perfumes and enters the eighth consciousness. Driven by the pull of karma, this consciousness is caused to enter and take up residence in a mother’s womb.

This is precisely the human soul-consciousness (*ātman-vijñāna*). Because there is the cause of action (*saṃskāra*), there is consciousness; therefore, it is said that "action is the condition for consciousness" (*saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam*).

Regarding "consciousness conditions name-and-form" (*vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam*): "name" (*nāma*) refers to the four mental factors of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, so called because they possess a designation but lack physical form or substance.
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the two drops—red and white—from the father and mother; these, together with one's own spiritual seed, coalesce with that red and white matter.
With craving as the cause, one receives the conception that forms the embryo. Its physical form is an illusory substance;

thus, regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), when consciousness first enters the womb, it coagulates into the state of *kalala*. Because there is consciousness, name-and-form exists by reason of it; hence it is said that "consciousness conditions name-and-form."
Regarding "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases" (*nāmarūpapratyayaṃ ṣaḍāyatanam*): the fetus develops from the coagulation of the *kalala*, and its six faculties (*indriya*) arise.

Because these faculties possess the meaning of "entering" (*āyatana*) toward their respective objects, they are called "bases. Since the six faculties are accomplished by means of name-and-form as their cause, it is said that "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases.

Regarding "the six sense bases condition contact" (*ṣaḍāyatanapratyayaḥ sparśaḥ*): once the faculties have formed and the being has emerged from the womb, up until the age of three or four, the faculties and their objects [interact].

Contact (*sparśa*). One has not yet fully understood this; it is merely the mutual touching of the two. Because contact exists due to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it is said that "the six sense bases are the condition for contact.
Regarding "contact conditions feeling" (*vedanā*): feeling is the act of experiencing or receiving. From the age of five or six...
Reaching the twelfth or thirteenth [week], due to the six objects of the senses coming into contact with the six sense organs, one immediately perceives external objects.

Although one is not yet able to give rise to a mind of craving and attachment, one is roughly capable of discerning matters such as the pleasant and the unpleasant. Because there is contact, there is reception.
Therefore it is said that "contact conditions feeling. These five [links] belong to the fruit of the present life. Regarding "feeling conditions craving":
from the ages of fourteen or fifteen up to eighteen or nineteen, one craves various excellent and wonderful requisites, as well as objects such as forms and sensual desires;
because of this experiencing [of feeling], craving immediately arises. Therefore it is said that "feeling conditions craving. Regarding "craving conditions grasping":
From the age of twenty onward, upon encountering all objects of desire, one gives rise to a mind of grasping and attachment, thinking to pursue them extensively and universally.

Because attachment arises from craving, it is said that "craving conditions grasping. Regarding "grasping conditions becoming": once one is attached to various objects, afflictions and karma become bound together;
good and evil take form, and cause and effect do not perish—this is called "becoming. This occurs because of craving and grasping.
Through accumulation and projection, causes give rise to the various realms of existence; hence it is said that "clinging conditions existence" (*upādāna-pratyaya-bhava*).

These three factors belong to the causes of the present life, and they further lead to the fruits of birth and death in the future. Regarding "existence conditions birth" (*bhava-pratyaya-jāti*), this refers to taking birth within the six destinies.
Since cause and effect do not perish, one is bound to a future life according to the characteristics of one's wholesome or unwholesome karma.

Because birth arises, it is said that "with birth as condition, there is arising. Regarding "with birth as condition, there is old age and death": the maturation and decay of the body that has taken birth is called old age and death.
Since once there is birth, one ultimately returns to old age and death, it is said that "with birth as condition, there is old age and death.

These two [links] belong to the results of the future world. These twelve factors are the dharma practiced by those who attain awakening through conditions (*pratyekabuddha*); they constitute the path of training.
This is the essential purport. Therefore, one should not weary of explaining it in detail. In short, although the various conditions are numerous, they all arise from ignorance (*avidyā*).
This ignorance is the root of birth and death and the foundation of saṃsāra. Those who wish to practice Prajñā should take the extinction of ignorance as their priority.
Only by means of the wisdom of Prajñā can one contemplate and clearly perceive [the nature of reality].
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is by nature fundamentally empty; it has no substantial reality. Thus, the nature of wisdom is truly pure, returning once more to wondrous stillness and penetrating clarity.
This is called the extinction of ignorance. When it is extinguished, there is no longer ignorance, nor is there any "ignorance" reaching a state of ultimate purity.
Once ignorance is exhausted, then everything from volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) down to consciousness (*vijñāna*) is likewise entirely exhausted. For...
If the root does not exist, where can the branches be attached? I know that there is no practice, nor is there an end to practice;

there is no consciousness, nor is there an end to consciousness; there is no name-and-form, nor is there an end to name-and-form; there are no six sense bases, nor is there an end to the six sense bases.
There is no contact, nor the exhaustion of contact; no feeling, nor the exhaustion of feeling; no craving, nor the exhaustion of craving;
no grasping, nor the exhaustion of grasping; no existence, nor the exhaustion of existence; no birth, nor the exhaustion of birth;
and so on, up to no aging and death, nor aging and death reaching the state of pure exhaustion. For when ignorance has ceased, then all outflows [are extinguished].

Exhausted of itself, affliction is spontaneously severed; the three poisons are naturally dissipated. The sins accumulated over ten thousand kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are all at once and suddenly stilled.
The very root of the cycle of birth and death is at once and suddenly eliminated. This is the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination.
This is the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas;
it is without suffering, accumulation, cessation, or the path.

Yet, it is not merely emptiness, for it concerns the twelve links of dependent origination. Thus, the fruit of the suffering of birth and death is called "suffering," referring to birth, old age, and so forth.
The five aggregates (skandhas) burn with the fires of birth, aging, sickness, and death; one encounters what is sought but cannot be found; one meets with the hated and the disliked;

and one is separated from the beloved—these eight sufferings manifest and oppress. The causes of delusion, karma, and suffering are called "accumulation" (samudaya), referring to the fetters of afflictions and karma that summon the eight sufferings.
Past accumulation leads to present suffering; present accumulation leads to future suffering. These two constitute the world.

This refers to cause and effect. The blissful fruit of *nirvāṇa* is called "cessation" (*nirodha*), meaning that when afflictions and karma are exhausted, the eight sufferings of birth and death are forever ended.

The causal path to this bliss is called the "path" (*mārga*), meaning that to remedy afflictions and karma, one must cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*).
These two constitute the supramundane cause and effect. For a detailed account of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, see the [relevant] fascicle.

In conclusion, those who preach these Four Noble Truths do so with the desire to cause sentient beings to know suffering and sever its origin, to aspire toward cessation and cultivate the path, thereby leaving suffering behind and attaining happiness.

This is the objective realm contemplated by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle. However, when Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas illuminate and realize this realm, they see that it is empty and quiescent in its very essence.
Not only are there no suffering and origin, but there is also no cessation and path. This is the emptiness of the Four [Noble Truths].
This is the truth. Herein there is no dharma of the śrāvakas;
there is neither wisdom nor attainment.
It is not only that the Four Truths are empty; for the wisdom that is able to contemplate is "wisdom," and the principle that is illuminated is "attainment."
These two are the dharmas of a bodhisattva. Speaking in terms of dharmas, the principle of wisdom is entirely emptiness;
there is no room for anything else to exist. That which exists is itself delusion; it is fundamentally non-existent. Speaking in terms of persons, this refers to those who cultivate prajñā.
When both subject and object are forgotten and both wisdom and principle are extinguished, this is the "non-existence of the capacity.

Since the non-existence of the capacity is exhausted, one has already accorded with primordial non-existence; how then could there be any attainment through wisdom? This is the emptiness of both person and phenomena.
Thus, there is no dharma of a bodhisattva. Such is the non-attainment within true emptiness.

This section, from "Therefore, in emptiness" up to this point, clarifies that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), one must fully realize that these aggregates (*skandha*) are empty and thereby restore the true essence.
It provides a detailed exposition of the phrase "the five aggregates are all empty" to accord with the intention of the Sovereign [Buddha].
The five aggregates reveal that there is no attainment, because there is nothing to be attained.
It is precisely because of this non-attainment that [the following follows]. Although this sentence serves as a transition from the preceding to the subsequent section.
Yet, there is nothing to be attained; this is the essential gateway for entering Prajñā and the great path for cultivating it.
Therefore, "non-attainment" is established as a distinct category to highlight its significance. Students should know what to take as their mirror.
Sixth, explaining the Bodhisattva according to their classification:
*Bodhisattva* is a Sanskrit term, abbreviated as *Pusa*. In the language of China, it means "Awakened Being" (Jue Youqing). *Tuo* is the pronunciation of *tuo*. Thus, the Bodhisattva arises.
First,
relying upon the *Prajñāpāramitā*,
one follows and adheres to the dharma-gate of reaching the other shore through wisdom, training therein and clearly perceiving the purity of intrinsic nature.
Because one has purified [the mind] and realized entry into true emptiness;
for this reason.
The mind is free from obstruction.
Therefore, it is not dragged or hindered by the various dharmas such as the aggregates (*skandhas*), nor is it blocked by various marks such as arising and ceasing.
It is pure and fundamental in nature, all-pervasive and sovereign.
Because there is no hindrance;
due to this mind being free from entanglement and obstruction,
there is no fear.

*Puyinbu* (怖音布): This means "fear. Sentient beings in the world, due to the hindrance of greedy attachment and delusion, dread the pursuit of birth and death and fear the obstructions of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Even those who practice supramundane dharmas, due to the hindrance of false yearning, give rise to fear toward this inherently illusory birth and death, and toward results that are not true.

Fear arises because the mind clings to superior views and the heart longs for wondrous realms. When the celestial Māras spy for an opportunity, they cause interference and disturbance, making people feel fearful together.
Once there is no longer any obstruction, the mind is free from the bonds of karma;
like the vast empty sky, what more could be feared? What more could be dreaded?
It is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions.

To be confused about the Truth is called "inversion" (*viparyāsa*); to pursue the false is called "perversion. A "dream" refers to the spirit wandering through illusory realms; it is because habitual tendencies from the past have not yet been extinguished.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the clinging to objects through distracted conceptualization; the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is deluded activity. All these are falsely constituted and entangled within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

they are the inverted perceptions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Even the dharmas of the truths and conditions cultivated by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are likewise inverted.
To aspire for illusory fruits is likewise like a dream. This is all fundamentally due to the inability to possess a mind free from hindrances. — Far [from liberation].

As for "detachment": all obstacles originally arise from entanglement and obstruction. Once entanglement and obstruction are empty, then the various obstacles of inverted dreams and delusions will naturally depart and recede to a great distance.
Ultimate nirvana.
Ultimately, one attains great parinirvāṇa; in great purity, one directly ascends to the other shore of all Buddhas.
○ Nirvana is called "great parinirvāṇa"; it is the place of great purity, the ground where there is neither birth nor extinction.
○ Seven: Clarifying the Buddhas According to the Three Periods of Time.
It is not only Bodhisattvas who cultivate and realize in this manner; rather, it applies to the Buddhas of these three periods: past, present, and future.
All Buddhas,
by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā,
give rise to their initial awakening; they likewise all rely upon this dharma-gate of reaching the other shore through wisdom for their practice.
Because of realizing true emptiness, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is why one achieves this fruit-stage of supreme, right, and perfect enlightenment. [In Sanskrit, *anuttara*...]
*Tāra* (多羅): In Chinese, it means "unsurpassed. *Samyak* (三藐): In Sanskrit, it means "perfectly equal" (*zhèngděng* 正等). *Sambodhi* (三菩提):
In Sanskrit, it means "perfect enlightenment" (*zhèngjué* 正覺). Bodhisattvas attain *nirvāṇa* by relying on *prajñā*;
all Buddhas attain *bodhi* by relying on *prajñā*. This is the path of great identity among all Buddhas and the source from which the myriad dharmas flow forth.
It is truly the Dharma of Prajñā!
△ Regarding the secret division, from the beginning until the end, it is known as the secret teaching within the secret; this is divided into three parts.
○ First, the section on the meaning of the mantra and the conclusion of the sutra.
Therefore, one knows that the Prajñāpāramitā—
by virtue of these causes and conditions— is the dharma-gate of reaching the other shore through wisdom; it is secret, wondrous,
and possesses the meaning of a mantra.
This is a great divine mantra.
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have falsely bound themselves with the dharmas of the five aggregates, the sense organs, and their objects;
these delusions are so powerful that they are difficult to shatter. When the wisdom of contemplation suddenly renders them empty, the efficacy of Prajñā is like a valiant divine army.
It can destroy all demons; it is the secret mantra of the Great Divinity.
It is the mantra of great illumination.

Its spiritual discernment is fully manifest, and its true principle is thoroughly penetrated. When both conditions and objects are discarded and both wisdom and attainment are simultaneously extinguished, then this is Prajñā.
Its efficacy is like a bright lamp through the long night, capable of destroying deep darkness; it is the secret mantra of great illumination, the unsurpassed mantra.
By relying upon it, Bodhisattvas attain ultimate Nirvana. Thus, the efficacy of Prajñā is both divine and luminous, capable of—
This is the secret mantra that reaches the ultimate pinnacle;
it is the peerless mantra.
It is by relying upon this that all Buddhas attain Bodhi; thus, the divine efficacy of Prajñā has no equal. This is not merely...
"Unsurpassed. This means that there is no secret mantra equal to it.
II. First, the section on the benefits of the mantra, which states:
"It can eliminate all suffering."
The efficacy of the Prajñā mantra is as vast as this: it can spontaneously eliminate all suffering and calamity in the world, enabling sentient beings to attain great happiness.
It is true and not false.
All that I have spoken is truthful speech, not something deceptive or illusory.
It is that which sentient beings should joyfully accept with faith and uphold as the excellent remedy for liberation from suffering; yet this requires the realization of true emptiness.

Those who are unable [to do so] reach this section by means of their own realization of non-attainment. It provides a detailed exposition on crossing over all suffering and distress, thereby responding to the intention of the Bodhisattvas.
The third section, "Identifying the Name and Reciting the Mantra," in ten parts, is hereby concluded.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-mantra is now spoken.
Such is the power of the Prajñā-mantra to eliminate suffering; for this reason, it is essential that this mantra be clearly articulated.

This is intended so that the great assembly may know it and thereby recite it. ○ This mantra takes secrecy as its essence, divine wonder as its function, and inconceivable resonance as its characteristic.
Its purpose is solely to cause people to receive benefit and joy, rather than to give rise to intellectual knowledge or visual perceptions; such is the meaning of this mantra.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
"Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. He spoke this mantra for all sentient beings to hear together.
This is a *dhāraṇī*. Traditionally, *dhāraṇīs* have never been translated [into Chinese]. Briefly, there are five meanings: first, they are the secret words of all Buddhas;
only Buddhas can understand one another, for these are not known by ordinary beings.

Second, they are *dhāraṇīs* (total retention); each individual word and phrase contains many meanings. Third, they may be the names of ghost-king deities; calling upon them commands them to provide protection.
They protect the practitioner. Fourth, they are the secret seals (*mudrā*) of all Buddhas; like a king’s official seal, there is nowhere they do not penetrate.
Fifth, they are sustained by inconceivable power; merely by reciting them in secret, one immediately obtains secret benefits. For these reasons, none are translated.
Commentators likewise provide no explanation at all, for fear that [the practitioner] might incur transgression. Great Master Kuang said: "Recently there have been..."
Regarding the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Mahākaruṇā*, and other dhāraṇīs, those who misinterpret the translations of Du [Shunzhi] destroy the Buddha-dharma; this is both laughable and lamentable.
They boast of being able to expound the secret teachings, yet they do not realize that they are precisely slandering the Tathāgata’s true wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, I have heard from Xianshou (Fazang) that the Sanskrit term *gate* means "crossing over" (*tú*). Moreover, as for the repeated utterance of *gate*:
It means to save oneself and to save others. "Pāra" in the Sanskrit language means "the other shore" (Chinese: *bī'àn*);

it signifies that the other shore can be reached by crossing over. "Saṃgha" in the Sanskrit language means "assembly" (*zhòng*) or "universal" (*pǔ*); it signifies that both self and others are universally saved, collectively reaching the other shore.

Regarding "bodhi": what kind of other shore is this? It refers to the station of the Great Bodhisattvas. "Sakya... [in the Sanskrit language... (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding "Sakya," which typically refers to the Śākya clan.)
*Baha*. This translates as "swift" or "expeditious. It means: "May that which is undertaken be swiftly accomplished.
Alternatively, it is said: *gate gate* signifies the Great Deity;
*pāragate* signifies the Great Illumination; *pārasaṃgate* signifies the Unsurpassed; and *bodhisatva*...
"Baha" (vāha) signifies "the peerless" (asama-sama). These two explanations seem plausible; for the time being, they are retained to satisfy the minds of those seeking understanding.

However, as they contravene the rule against translating [certain terms], I have not dared to include them in the formal commentary. In short, the reasons for not translating mantra-syllables are twofold:
first, to clarify that the characteristics of verbal expression are empty; second, to clarify the characteristics of the mind's objects of perception.
The emptiness [of dharmas] intends to cause people to sever the path of verbal expression and to still the mind of discursive thought, for all phenomena return to the One.
Furthermore, as for "mantras" (dhāraṇīs): they take the essential meaning of the entire sutra and condense it within a few words of esoteric speech.
Thus, the sutra is the exoteric teaching of the mantra, and the mantra is the esoteric teaching of the sutra. To maintain both together is to possess the excellence of both.
Complete. Whether recited individually or combined, they encompass one another without omission. To uphold the mantra is to uphold the sutra; to understand the sutra is to understand the mantra.
Thus, there is truly no need to forcefully seek their interpretation or explanation.
The final section consists of incantations that collectively conclude the entire text.
○ Appendix:
The Thirty-Seven Factors of Enlightenment. These refer to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, and the five faculties.
The powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. As for the four foundations of mindfulness, they are: the body, sensation, the mind, and phenomena.

Indeed, the Buddha revealed these as the wisdom for entering contemplation through skillful means. One must contemplate the body as impure, contemplate sensation as suffering, contemplate the mind as impermanent, and contemplate phenomena as selfless.
This is the very first step for entering the state of sainthood from that of an ordinary person.

The skill of walking down the path consists of uninterrupted mindfulness at every moment; hence it is called the "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). As for the "four right efforts" (*samyakprahāṇa*):
one diligently strives so that evil already committed does not increase, diligently strives so that evil not yet committed does not arise, and [diligently strives so that] good already committed...
One should diligently cause [wholesome states] to increase. One should diligently cause unperformed virtues to arise. As for the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*):

they are concentration (*samādhi*), mind (*citta*), exertion (*vīrya*), and self-mastery (*ātman*). Concentration means the complete severance of afflictions. Mind means remaining constantly in mindfulness.

Exertion means being uninterrupted for even a single moment. Self-mastery means bringing [the practice] into a single unified whole. As for the five faculties (*indriya*): the faculty of faith (*śraddhā*) and the faculty of exertion (*vīrya*).
The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). This means:

having faith without doubt, exerting effort without retreating, maintaining mindfulness without ceasing, being concentrated without distraction, and possessing wisdom without sinking. The five powers (*pañcabala*) are: the power of faith, the power of exertion, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are: mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, exertion, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity. Mindfulness...

This means that the mind and mental factors do not abide; they do not cease for even a single moment. "Discernment" (vicaya) refers to the selection between the true and the false, being able to distinguish between black and red.
"Exertion" (vīrya) means being direct and not crooked, possessing courage and freedom from deviousness. "Joy" (prīti) refers to attaining the bliss of dhyāna.
"Throughout the body there is leaping joy. "Lightness" means that worldly toil is suddenly stilled and the mind attains sovereignty. "Stability" means the roots are buried ten feet deep;
the eight winds cannot move them. "Renunciation" means the faculties and their objects are liberated, such that the cycle of rebirth is no longer continued.
The Eightfold Noble Path consists of right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

Right view is the absence of views concerning oneness or difference, existence or non-existence, annihilation or permanence, and so forth. Right thought is the emptiness of the six consciousnesses and the purity of the mental faculty (*manas*).
Right speech is the chanting of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; it is the purity of the mouth. Right action is the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; it is the purity of the body.
"Purity" means to follow the wisdom of the Buddha and enter the stream of the sages. "Right Effort" means to be refined and unmixed, without shrinking from weariness.
"Right Mindfulness" means to have a single mind without distraction, applying oneself with ever-increasing urgency.
Right concentration transcends all states of existence, including the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
